_link.title: I can explain how a mass spectrometer uses electric and magnetic fields to separate ions by mass

toLevel2.stem: What is the purpose of a mass spectrometer?
toLevel2.answer: To separate and identify ions by their mass
distractors: To measure the speed of light in a vacuum
To accelerate particles to the speed of light
To generate strong magnetic fields for motors

toLevel2.stem: In a mass spectrometer, what type of field accelerates the ions to a known speed?
distractors: A magnetic field
A gravitational field
A thermal radiation field

toLevel2.stem: In the deflection region of a mass spectrometer, what causes ions to follow curved paths?
distractors: An electric field
A gravitational field
Collisions with gas atoms

toLevel2.stem: In a mass spectrometer, which ions curve more tightly in the magnetic field?
distractors: Heavier ions
Faster ions
Ions with less charge

toLevel2.stem: Which formula gives the radius of an ion's path in the deflection region of a mass spectrometer?
distractors: r = qB/(mv)
r = qvB/m
r = mB/(qv)

toLevel2.stem: In a mass spectrometer, ions are first {{blank:1}} by an electric field, then {{blank:2}} by a magnetic field.
Heavier ions follow paths with a {{blank:1}} radius, while lighter ions follow paths with a {{blank:2}} radius.
The radius of an ion's path depends on its {{blank:1}}, speed, charge, and the {{blank:2}} field strength.
In a mass spectrometer, heavier ions follow a circular path with a smaller radius than lighter ions.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: A mass spectrometer uses both electric and magnetic fields to identify ions by their mass.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Why must ions have the same speed before entering the deflection region of a mass spectrometer?
toLevel3.answer: So that differences in radius are due to mass alone, not speed
distractors: So that all ions arrive at the detector at exactly the same time
So that the magnetic field can exert a force on all the ions equally
So that the ions do not collide with each other inside the device

toLevel3.stem: Two isotopes of neon (Ne-20 and Ne-22) enter the deflection region at the same speed and charge. Which isotope has a larger radius?
toLevel3.answer: Ne-22, because it has a greater mass
distractors: Ne-20, because lighter particles curve less
Both have the same radius because they have the same charge
Ne-22, because it has a greater charge

toLevel3.stem: How does the detector in a mass spectrometer determine which ions are present in a sample?
toLevel3.answer: By measuring where ions land, since different masses follow different radii and hit the detector at different positions
distractors: By measuring the colour of light emitted when ions strike the detector surface material
By measuring the speed of each ion as it arrives at the detector after deflection
By counting the total number of ions that reach the detector without any deflection

toLevel3.stem: Why must a mass spectrometer operate in a vacuum?
toLevel3.answer: To prevent ions from colliding with air molecules, which would scatter them and blur the results
distractors: To ensure the magnetic field is strong enough to deflect the ions in the chamber
To prevent the electric field from being absorbed by the air inside the device
To allow the detector to function because it only works in the absence of air

toLevel3.stem: What information can be obtained from the mass spectrum produced by a mass spectrometer?
toLevel3.answer: The masses of the ions present and their relative abundances in the sample
distractors: The colours of the elements present in the sample being analysed in the device
The temperature at which each element melts and boils under standard conditions
The chemical reactions that the sample can undergo when heated in the laboratory

toLevel3.stem: In the formula r = mv/(qB), what effect does increasing the magnetic field strength have on the separation of two isotopes?
toLevel3.answer: Both radii decrease, but the separation between landing positions may change depending on geometry
distractors: Both radii increase, making the isotopes harder to distinguish on the detector
Only the lighter isotope's radius decreases while the heavier one stays the same
The magnetic field has no effect on radius because it only changes the speed

toLevel3.stem: A velocity selector or accelerating voltage ensures all ions have the same {{blank:1}} before entering the {{blank:2}} region.
The mass spectrum shows {{blank:1}} on the x-axis and relative {{blank:2}} on the y-axis.
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 can be distinguished because their different {{blank:1}} produce different {{blank:2}} in the magnetic field.
A mass spectrometer must operate in a vacuum to prevent collisions between ions and air molecules.
distractors: False

toLevel4.stem: Singly charged ions of two isotopes (mass 28 u and 30 u) enter a mass spectrometer at 1.0 × 10⁵ m/s in a 0.50 T field. Calculate the difference in their radii. (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
distractors: Approximately 0.041 m
Approximately 0.41 m
Approximately 0.00041 m

toLevel4.stem: An ion of mass 3.82 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C enters a 0.40 T field at 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s. What is the radius of its path?
In a mass spectrometer, ions are accelerated from rest through 500 V. A singly charged ion lands at a radius of 0.15 m in a 0.30 T field. What is the mass of the ion?
toLevel4.answer: Use qV = ½mv² to find v, then m = qBr/v to find mass
distractors: Use F = qvB directly to find mass without needing the velocity
Mass cannot be determined because both v and m are unknown
Use r = mv/(qB) with v = E/B to find mass from fields alone

toLevel4.stem: A doubly charged ion (q = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) has the same mass and speed as a singly charged ion (q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). Compare their radii in the same field.
toLevel4.answer: The doubly charged ion has half the radius
distractors: Both ions have the same radius of deflection
The doubly charged ion has twice the radius
The doubly charged ion has a quarter of radius

toLevel4.stem: Why does the mass spectrometer actually measure the mass-to-charge ratio (m/q) rather than the mass alone?
toLevel4.answer: The radius depends on m/q, not m alone, so ions with different charges but the same m/q follow the same path
distractors: The charge of every ion is always the same so m/q is equivalent to measuring m directly
The mass spectrometer cannot detect charge at all so it can only measure the ratio m/q
The charge is measured separately by a different device so only m/q comes from the radius

toLevel4.stem: Two ions have the same m/q ratio but different charges. How do they appear in a mass spectrometer?
toLevel4.answer: They follow the same radius and land at the same position, appearing as a single peak
distractors: They follow different radii and land at different positions on the mass spectrometer detector
They follow the same radius but arrive at different times producing separate detector peaks
They cannot both exist because no two ions can have the same m/q with different charges

toLevel4.stem: A mass spectrometer is used to analyse a sample containing three isotopes with masses 63 u, 64 u, and 65 u. Predict the pattern on the detector.
toLevel4.answer: Three separate spots at slightly different positions, with the 65 u isotope landing furthest from the entrance
distractors: A single spot because the mass differences are too small for the detector to resolve them
Three spots with the 63 u isotope landing furthest from the entrance slit of the device
Two spots because 64 u lands exactly between 63 u and 65 u and cannot be distinguished

toLevel4.stem: A doubly charged ion has {{blank:1}} the radius of a singly charged ion of the same mass and speed because r is inversely proportional to {{blank:2}}.
The mass spectrometer actually measures {{blank:1}} rather than mass alone, so ions must be {{blank:2}} charged to give meaningful results.
Heavier isotopes land {{blank:1}} from the entrance slit because they follow arcs with {{blank:2}} radii.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the advantage of using a time-of-flight mass spectrometer over a magnetic deflection mass spectrometer for analysing large biological molecules.
toLevel5.answer: Time-of-flight avoids the need for large magnetic fields and can analyse very heavy molecules that would require impractically large deflection radii
distractors: Time-of-flight is less accurate but cheaper, making it suitable only for rough measurements
Magnetic deflection is always superior because it directly measures mass without calculation
Time-of-flight cannot analyse biological molecules because they are too heavy to be ionised

toLevel5.stem: A mass spectrometer detects two peaks at radii of 0.120 m and 0.132 m. If the lighter ion has mass 20 u, calculate the mass of the heavier ion.
Analyse why the resolution of a mass spectrometer (its ability to distinguish ions of similar masses) improves with a stronger magnetic field.
toLevel5.answer: Stronger fields produce smaller radii, but the absolute difference in radii between ions of different masses is maintained, making the angular separation larger
distractors: Stronger fields increase the radii of all ions making them easier to see on the detector
Stronger fields do not improve resolution; only the detector sensitivity matters for this
Stronger fields increase the speed of the ions which makes them land more precisely always

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that a mass spectrometer could identify the element by detecting only one isotope. Evaluate the limitations of this approach.
toLevel5.answer: Many elements have overlapping m/q values for different isotopes; the full isotope pattern provides a more reliable identification
distractors: The approach is perfectly reliable because every isotope has a unique mass that identifies it
The approach is wrong because mass spectrometers cannot detect individual isotopes at all
The approach works only for elements with one stable isotope and fails for all other elements

toLevel5.stem: Compare how a mass spectrometer and a velocity selector use the relationship between electric and magnetic forces, and explain their different purposes.
toLevel5.answer: A velocity selector balances forces to pass one speed; a mass spectrometer uses the magnetic force alone to separate by mass after speed is fixed
distractors: Both devices use identical setups of crossed fields; they differ only in detector placement
A velocity selector separates by mass while a mass spectrometer selects particles by speed
Both devices balance electric and magnetic forces; neither uses one type of field alone

toLevel5.stem: In carbon dating, a mass spectrometer measures the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12. Explain why the mass spectrometer is well-suited for this measurement.
toLevel5.answer: The 2 u mass difference produces measurably different radii, and the detector can quantify relative amounts of each isotope
distractors: The mass spectrometer measures the radioactivity of carbon-14 directly from its decay rate
The mass spectrometer counts individual atoms by weighing them on an extremely precise scale
The mass spectrometer identifies carbon-14 by its colour which differs from carbon-12 visually

toLevel5.stem: A mass spectrometer uses a 0.80 T field and detects a singly charged ion at radius 0.25 m. The ion was accelerated through 1000 V. Calculate the mass of the ion.
distractors: Approximately 3.2 × 10⁻²⁶ kg
Approximately 1.3 × 10⁻²⁵ kg
Approximately 6.4 × 10⁻²⁵ kg

toLevel5.stem: Predict what would happen if the magnetic field in a mass spectrometer were not uniform across the deflection region.
toLevel5.answer: Ion paths would not be perfectly semicircular, reducing measurement accuracy and making mass identification less precise
distractors: The spectrometer would work identically because only the average field strength matters
All ions would follow straight lines because non-uniform fields cannot produce curvature
The spectrometer would separate ions by charge instead of mass in a non-uniform field

toLevel5.stem: The ratio of radii for two isotopes equals the ratio of their {{blank:1}}, allowing the mass spectrometer to {{blank:2}} them on the detector.
In carbon dating, the mass spectrometer distinguishes carbon-12 from carbon-14 because their different {{blank:1}} produce different {{blank:2}} in the deflection field.
